before.clue: Their plan aimed to prevent one outcome. Ironically, that exact outcome followed the disruption. What happened to the people?
before.fact: Jehovah scattered the builders across the earth—the very outcome they had tried to avoid. Their plan produced the opposite result. (Genesis 11:4, 8)
before.hint: They could not stay together as one population.

after.clue: The builders wanted to stay together. What happened to them across the earth after their language was confused?
after.fact: Jehovah scattered the builders across the earth—the very outcome they had tried to avoid. Their plan produced the opposite result. (Genesis 11:4, 8)
after.hint: They could not stay together as one population.
after.narration: Construction stops and the people spread out. The very outcome they'd wanted to prevent becomes part of the story.

records.reviewNote: Genesis links Babel to confusion of language. The hint distinguishes the Bible’s name explanation from a generic city fact.

before.clue: The unfinished ambition left behind a place-name connected with failed understanding. What was it?
before.fact: The name Babel became tied to the confusion of language. The chapter connects a grand human project with the limits of human ambition. (Genesis 11:9)
before.hint: Genesis 11:9 records the city’s name after the languages were disrupted.

after.clue: Which city got a name linked with the confusion of the people's language?
after.fact: Genesis connects the city's name with Jehovah's confusing their language. They'd wanted to make a celebrated name for themselves, but their city became known for what happened to their speech. (Genesis 11:4, 9)
after.hint: Its name is linked with the Hebrew verb meaning to confuse.
after.narration: The city receives a name connected with what happened to the people's language. Genesis ties the name to Jehovah's action.

records.reviewNote: Daniel 1 supplies a recognizable Chaldean context for the hint; the migration itself follows Genesis 11. No invented Ur landmark.

before.clue: Abram’s family left an established Mesopotamian city identified by a people group. What group completed the name “Ur of the ___”?
before.fact: Leaving Ur meant leaving an established home, not just moving camps. Abram’s journey begins with his family heading toward an unfamiliar destination. (Genesis 11:31)
before.hint: Genesis 11:28 identifies the people associated with Ur.

after.clue: Abram's hometown was called Ur of the ___. Which people's name completes it?
after.fact: Leaving Ur meant leaving an established home, not just moving camps. Abram’s journey begins with his family heading toward an unfamiliar destination. (Genesis 11:31)
after.hint: Their language and writing later formed part of Daniel's education in Babylon.
after.narration: Terah's household leaves Ur with Canaan as its destination. Abram travels with Sarai and his nephew Lot.

records.reviewNote: Acts 7 clarifies the call before the Haran stay; Genesis 11–12 supplies Terah’s stop and Abram’s later departure.

before.clue: Abram’s journey unfolded in stages. Where did the family settle before the journey toward Canaan resumed?
before.fact: The family stopped in Haran before Abram continued. Faithful journeys can have stages; this one did not unfold in a single move. (Genesis 11:31–12:4)
before.hint: Terah died at this intermediate location (Genesis 11:32).

after.clue: Abram’s journey unfolded in stages. Where did the family settle before the journey toward Canaan resumed?
after.fact: The family stopped in Haran before Abram continued. Faithful journeys can have stages; this one did not unfold in a single move. (Genesis 11:31–12:4)
after.hint: Terah died at this intermediate location (Genesis 11:32).
after.narration: The family settles along the way instead of reaching Canaan in one move. After Terah's death, Abram will continue the journey.

records.reviewNote: Sarai’s childlessness makes the nation promise meaningful. Added Genesis 11:30 to support that contrast.

before.clue: Abram was still childless, yet Jehovah described a future far larger than one household. What would his descendants become?
before.fact: Jehovah promised to make Abram a great nation even though the family’s future was uncertain. The promise looked beyond what Abram could already see. (Genesis 12:1–2)
before.hint: It would be an entire people with a shared identity.

after.clue: Abram was still childless, yet Jehovah described a future far larger than one household. What would his descendants become?
after.fact: Jehovah promised to make Abram a great nation even though the family’s future was uncertain. The promise looked beyond what Abram could already see. (Genesis 12:1–2)
after.hint: It would be an entire people with a shared identity.
after.narration: Sarai has no child, yet Jehovah makes a promise about a people who will come from Abram. The promise looks far beyond the household as it is now.

records.reviewNote: The promise reaches families of the ground beyond Abram’s household. The hint asks the player to notice its scope.

before.clue: Jehovah’s promise through Abram reached beyond his own descendants. Which groups throughout the earth would benefit?
before.fact: The blessing promised through Abram would reach all families of the ground. His journey was connected to a purpose far greater than one household. (Genesis 12:3)
before.hint: The scope crossed national and household boundaries.

after.clue: Jehovah’s promise through Abram reached beyond his own descendants. Which groups throughout the earth would benefit?
after.fact: The blessing promised through Abram would reach all families of the ground. His journey was connected to a purpose far greater than one household. (Genesis 12:3)
after.hint: Think of related people in households, rather than kings or nations.
after.narration: Jehovah's words reach beyond Abram's own descendants. People throughout the earth are included in the blessing he describes.

records.reviewNote: Sarai is Abram’s wife at departure; the clue distinguishes her earlier name from Sarah and cites the later change.

before.clue: The promise involved a couple facing an uncertain future, not a lone traveler. Who left home alongside Abram?
before.fact: Sarai left with Abram on the journey toward Canaan. The account involves a family stepping away from a known home into a promised future. (Genesis 12:4–5)
before.hint: This was Abram’s wife before her later name change.

after.clue: Abram didn't travel alone. What was his wife's name before Jehovah later changed it?
after.fact: Sarai left with Abram on the journey toward Canaan. The account involves a family stepping away from a known home into a promised future. (Genesis 12:4–5)
after.hint: This was Abram’s wife before her later name change.
after.narration: Abram leaves with his wife and nephew, along with their possessions and the people they'd acquired. This is a household on the move.

records.reviewNote: Lot is Abram’s nephew, not his son. The wording asks about that specific traveler without treating the whole household as a small party.

before.clue: Abram took responsibility for a younger family member on his journey. Which nephew came with him?
before.fact: Lot accompanied Abram into Canaan. That shared journey sets up later choices that would separate their households. (Genesis 12:4–5; 13:5–11)
before.hint: This relative later faced an important choice over pastureland.

after.clue: Which nephew traveled with Abram into Canaan?
after.fact: Lot accompanied Abram into Canaan. That shared journey sets up later choices that would separate their households. (Genesis 12:4–5; 13:5–11)
after.hint: This relative later faced an important choice over pastureland.
after.narration: A younger relative travels with Abram. Their shared journey will lead to important decisions about where their households live.

records.reviewNote: They arrive in Canaan while Canaanites live there. The reference covers both departure and arrival; no immediate-possession claim.

before.clue: Abram accepted a future he could not yet see clearly. Which land did his journey ultimately lead him into?
before.fact: Abram arrived in Canaan, but others were already living there. The promised land was not simply handed over as an empty territory. (Genesis 12:5–7)
before.hint: Jehovah later promised this territory to Abram’s offspring.

after.clue: Abram accepted a future he could not yet see clearly. Which land did his journey ultimately lead him into?
after.fact: Abram arrived in Canaan, but others were already living there. The promised land was not simply handed over as an empty territory. (Genesis 12:5–7)
after.hint: Jehovah later promised this territory to Abram’s offspring.
after.narration: The travelers reach the land Jehovah promised to show Abram. Other people already live there, and the promise still looks ahead to his offspring.

records.reviewNote: Shechem’s geography comes from Insight; Jehovah’s appearance and the offspring promise are explicit in Genesis 12:6–7.

before.clue: On reaching the promised land, Abram stopped near the big trees of Moreh. What nearby place marks this early moment?
before.fact: At Shechem, Jehovah promised the land to Abram’s offspring while Canaanites still occupied it. The visible circumstances and the promise were not yet the same. (Genesis 12:6–7)
before.hint: The settlement is identified in Genesis 12:6.

after.clue: On reaching the promised land, Abram stopped near the big trees of Moreh. What nearby place marks this early moment?
after.fact: Canaanites were living in the land when Jehovah promised it to Abram's offspring. Abram built an altar there, but the promise would be fulfilled in the future. Arriving in Canaan and receiving it as an inheritance were different things. (Genesis 12:6–7)
after.hint: This city stood in the valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
after.narration: Abram stops near the big trees of Moreh. Here Jehovah appears to him and speaks about giving the land to his offspring.

records.reviewNote: The altar follows Jehovah’s appearance. Removed the claim to know Abram’s inner motive, while retaining its worship function.

before.clue: After Jehovah appeared to Abram, he made his gratitude tangible. What did he construct for worship?
before.fact: Abram built an altar after receiving the promise. Worship marked an important point in his journey before he moved farther on. (Genesis 12:7)
before.hint: It was a place for offering sacrifices, not a home or a tower.

after.clue: After Jehovah appeared to Abram, what did Abram build for worship?
after.fact: Abram built an altar after receiving the promise. Worship marked an important point in his journey before he moved farther on. (Genesis 12:7)
after.hint: It was a place for offering sacrifices, not a home or a tower.
after.narration: After Jehovah appears to Abram, Abram builds something used in worship. It marks this stage of his journey before he moves on.

records.reviewNote: Bethel means House of God. The geographic clue retains Ai to the east and does not confuse Abram’s stop with Jacob’s later dream.

before.clue: Abram later camped between Ai and a town to its west, where he called on Jehovah’s name. Which town?
before.fact: Near Bethel, Abram again built an altar and called on Jehovah’s name. His worship continued as the journey continued. (Genesis 12:8–9)
before.hint: Genesis 12:8 identifies the place west of Ai.

after.clue: Abram later camped between Ai and a town to its west, where he called on Jehovah’s name. Which town?
after.fact: Near Bethel, Abram again built an altar and called on Jehovah’s name. His worship continued as the journey continued. (Genesis 12:8–9)
after.hint: The town's name means House of God. It lay west of Ai.
after.narration: Abram pitches his tent between two towns, with Ai to the east. He again builds an altar and calls on Jehovah's name.

records.reviewNote: The basket is papyrus coated with bitumen and pitch, not an uncoated drifting cradle. The explanation adds the three-month concealment.

before.clue: What carried baby Moses beside the river?
before.fact: Jochebed placed her baby in a prepared papyrus basket among reeds by the Nile.
before.hint: The baby was laid inside a little waterproof container.

after.clue: What carried baby Moses beside the river?
after.fact: Moses' mother used a papyrus basket coated with bitumen and pitch. She placed it among the reeds after she could no longer keep him concealed. The account describes preparation and care, not simply putting a baby into the river. (Exodus 2:1–3)
after.hint: The baby was laid inside a little waterproof container.
after.narration: A mother has kept her baby concealed for three months. When she can no longer do so, she prepares a coated papyrus container and places him among the riverbank plants.

records.reviewNote: The Nile bank is the placement, not the middle of an uncontrolled current. The explanation includes Pharaoh’s daughter coming to bathe.

before.clue: Beside which river was the basket placed?
before.fact: The basket was placed among reeds along the bank of the Nile.
before.hint: Egypt’s great river provided the setting for this account.

after.clue: Beside which river was the basket placed?
after.fact: The basket was placed among reeds along the Nile's bank. Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe in that same river and noticed it. The location connects the mother's careful preparation with what happened next. (Exodus 2:3–5)
after.hint: Egypt’s great river provided the setting for this account.
after.narration: The prepared container is placed along the bank of Egypt's great river. Pharaoh's daughter will come down to bathe in the same place.

records.reviewNote: Reeds are the riverbank plants surrounding the basket. The explanation links that location to the sister’s watch.

before.clue: What plants sheltered the basket?
before.fact: The reeds along the riverbank concealed the basket.
before.hint: The basket was placed among tall plants growing near the riverbank.

after.clue: What plants sheltered the basket?
after.fact: The basket lay among the reeds by the riverbank, and Pharaoh's daughter caught sight of it there. The account gives us that specific setting; it doesn't say the basket drifted downstream. (Exodus 2:3–5)
after.hint: The basket was placed among tall plants growing near the riverbank.
after.narration: The baby has been placed at the river's edge, among the plants growing there. His sister watches from a distance.

records.reviewNote: Exodus calls the watcher his sister. The explanation makes her proposal for a Hebrew nurse part of the rescue sequence.

before.clue: Who watched what would happen to the baby?
before.fact: Moses’ sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him.
before.hint: Someone from his own family watched the basket from a distance.

after.clue: Who watched what would happen to the baby?
after.fact: Moses' sister watched from a distance. When Pharaoh's daughter found him, she stepped forward and offered to find a Hebrew woman to nurse him. Watching became an opportunity to help. (Exodus 2:4–8)
after.hint: Someone from his own family watched the basket from a distance.
after.narration: A member of the baby's own family stays nearby to see what will happen. Her attention will soon lead to a chance to help.

records.reviewNote: Numbers 26:59 and Insight identify Miriam; Exodus 15 supports her later musical role. The hint separates the unnamed watcher from her later name.

before.clue: What was the name of Moses’ sister?
before.fact: Miriam watched over her little brother from a distance.
before.hint: The sister’s name also appears in Exodus 15:20.

after.clue: What was the name of Moses’ sister?
after.fact: Exodus calls the watching girl Moses' sister; Numbers identifies Miriam as his sister by name. She helped bring their mother back to nurse the baby. Much later, she led Israel's women in song after the Red Sea crossing. (Exodus 2:4–8; Numbers 26:59; Exodus 15:20–21)
after.hint: She later led Israel's women in song with tambourines after the Red Sea crossing.
after.narration: The watching sister steps forward when Pharaoh's daughter finds the baby. Another Bible passage identifies this sister by name.

records.reviewNote: Pharaoh’s daughter recognizes a Hebrew baby and feels compassion, both explicit. The explanation shows why accepting a nurse matters.

before.clue: Pharaoh’s ______ noticed the basket.
before.fact: Pharaoh’s daughter saw the basket among the reeds and felt compassion for the baby.
before.hint: She was a royal member of Pharaoh’s family, not his wife.

after.clue: Pharaoh’s ______ noticed the basket.
after.fact: Pharaoh's daughter recognized the crying baby as a Hebrew and felt compassion for him. She agreed to the sister's suggestion of a Hebrew nurse. That brought the baby's own mother into the arrangements. (Exodus 2:5–9)
after.hint: She was a royal member of Pharaoh’s family, not his wife.
after.narration: A woman from Pharaoh's household sees the crying Hebrew baby and feels compassion. She is willing to hear the sister's suggestion about finding a nurse.

records.reviewNote: The girl sent for the basket is the attendant, distinct from Moses’ sister. The clue and explanation guard against conflating them.

before.clue: A slave ____ was sent to fetch the basket.
before.fact: A slave girl retrieved the basket. Later, Miriam helped arrange for the baby to be cared for.
before.hint: One of the young women attending Pharaoh’s daughter retrieved the basket.

after.clue: Which young attendant did Pharaoh's daughter send to get the basket? A slave ___.
after.fact: Pharaoh's daughter sent her slave girl to fetch the basket. Moses' sister then offered to find a nurse, and called his mother. These were different girls with different parts in the rescue. (Exodus 2:5–8)
after.hint: One of the young women attending Pharaoh’s daughter retrieved the basket.
after.narration: Pharaoh's daughter sends an attendant to get the container. The baby's sister has a different part to play in what follows.

records.reviewNote: Moses identifies with the Hebrews whose burdens he sees. The explanation connects the occupation clue with the act of oppression.

before.clue: Who was being beaten when Moses intervened in Egypt?
before.fact: Moses saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his own people.
before.hint: Think of the Israelites living under Egyptian rule.

after.clue: Who was being beaten when Moses intervened in Egypt?
after.fact: Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. He had gone out to look at the burdens his brothers were bearing. The event brought him face to face with their harsh treatment. (Exodus 2:11)
after.hint: Think of the Israelites living under Egyptian rule.
after.narration: Moses goes out to see the burdens his own people are bearing. He encounters an act of harsh treatment.

records.reviewNote: Moses kills the Egyptian and hides him in the sand. The text stays factual and restrained, without celebrating the killing.

before.clue: What was the nationality of the man Moses struck after seeing the abuse?
before.fact: Moses struck the Egyptian who had been beating a Hebrew. The account does not praise killing or describe it graphically.
before.hint: He was part of the ruling nation, not an Israelite.

after.clue: What was the nationality of the man Moses struck after seeing the abuse?
after.fact: Moses killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. The next day, another man referred to what he'd done, and Moses realized it was known. His action had consequences he couldn't keep hidden. (Exodus 2:11–14)
after.hint: He was part of the ruling nation, not an Israelite.
after.narration: Moses intervenes and kills the man who has been beating one of his people. He hides the body, but the incident will become known.

records.reviewNote: Pharaoh seeks to kill Moses after hearing of the incident. The explanation makes the flight’s cause clear.

before.clue: Who learned what Moses had done and sought to kill him?
before.fact: Pharaoh heard about the incident and tried to have Moses killed. Moses fled from Egypt.
before.hint: The ruler of Egypt.

after.clue: Who learned what Moses had done and sought to kill him?
after.fact: Pharaoh tried to kill Moses after hearing what had happened. Moses fled to Midian. This wasn't an orderly move to a new home; the account connects his departure with a threat to his life. (Exodus 2:14–15)
after.hint: The ruler of Egypt.
after.narration: The report reaches Egypt's ruler, and Moses' life is threatened. Staying in Egypt is no longer safe for him.

records.reviewNote: Midian is the destination after leaving Egypt. The explanation connects that move with the well and new household.

before.clue: To what land did Moses flee?
before.fact: Moses escaped to the land of Midian, where the next part of his life unfolded.
before.hint: A land where Moses would meet a priest and his daughters.

after.clue: To what land did Moses flee?
after.fact: Moses fled to Midian and sat down by a well. There he would meet the daughters of a local priest. The place where he stopped after escaping Egypt became the setting for the next part of his life. (Exodus 2:15–16)
after.hint: A land where Moses would meet a priest and his daughters.
after.narration: Moses escapes from Egypt and stops by a well in another land. This stop introduces the people who will become part of his new life.

records.reviewNote: The well introduces the priest’s seven daughters and their flock. The explanation adds the daily task rather than repeating the answer.

before.clue: Where was Moses sitting when the priest’s daughters arrived?
before.fact: Moses sat down by a well. Seven daughters of the priest of Midian came to draw water for their father’s flock.
before.hint: People came here to draw water for their flocks.

after.clue: Where was Moses sitting when the priest’s daughters arrived?
after.fact: The priest of Midian's seven daughters came to the well to draw water for their father's flock. When shepherds drove them away, Moses helped them and watered the flock. An ordinary watering place became a place to stand up for others. (Exodus 2:15–17)
after.hint: People came here to draw water for their flocks.
after.narration: Seven daughters of a local priest arrive to draw water for their father's flock. Moses is sitting at the place where they come to work.

records.reviewNote: Shepherds drive the women away; Moses helps and waters the flock. The explanation uses only the actions Exodus records.

before.clue: Who tried to drive the women away from the water?
before.fact: Other shepherds drove the women away. Moses stood up for them and helped water their flock.
before.hint: They looked after livestock, but did not treat the women kindly.

after.clue: Who tried to drive the women away from the water?
after.fact: The shepherds drove the women away, but Moses helped them and watered their flock. The women got home so quickly that their father asked what had happened! Their answer led him to invite Moses for a meal. (Exodus 2:17–20)
after.hint: They looked after livestock, but did not treat the women kindly.
after.narration: The women are driven away from the water. Moses gets up to help them and waters their flock.

records.reviewNote: God hears the enslaved Israelites and remembers his covenant. The explanation connects the transition to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob without implying forgetfulness.

before.clue: What did God do when the Israelites groaned under slavery?
before.fact: Jehovah heard the Israelites’ groaning, remembered his covenant, and paid attention to them.
before.hint: Their suffering did not go unnoticed.

after.clue: What did God do when the Israelites groaned under slavery?
after.fact: God heard the Israelites' groaning and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Their suffering hadn't gone unnoticed. The account ties the coming rescue to a promise that was already in place. (Exodus 2:23–25)
after.hint: Their suffering did not go unnoticed.
after.narration: Back in Egypt, the Israelites continue to groan under slavery. The account turns to God's attention to their suffering and his covenant.

records.reviewNote: Moses is tending Jethro’s flock when he reaches Horeb. The explanation grounds the encounter in his ordinary work.

before.clue: What was Moses looking after while working as a shepherd?
before.fact: Moses was shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, priest of Midian.
before.hint: Sheep and other animals kept by a shepherd.

after.clue: What was Moses looking after while working as a shepherd?
after.fact: Moses was caring for his father-in-law Jethro's flock when he reached Horeb. This remarkable encounter began during his ordinary work as a shepherd. (Exodus 3:1–4)
after.hint: Sheep and other animals kept by a shepherd.
after.narration: Moses is working as a shepherd for his father-in-law Jethro. As he leads the animals through the wilderness, he reaches Horeb.

records.reviewNote: The bush burns without being consumed; Moses turns to inspect it. The explanation does not confuse the plant with the angel speaking.

before.clue: What burned without being consumed?
before.fact: Jehovah’s angel appeared to Moses in a flame in the middle of a thornbush. The bush did not burn up.
before.hint: A thorny plant, not a tree.

after.clue: What burned without being consumed?
after.fact: The thornbush was on fire without being consumed. That unusual sight made Moses go closer to investigate. It was then that God called to him from the bush. (Exodus 3:2–4)
after.hint: A thorny plant, not a tree.
after.narration: Moses sees flames, yet the plant in their midst isn't being consumed. He goes closer to investigate.

records.reviewNote: Removing sandals responds to holy ground. The explanation follows God’s instruction instead of inventing a custom’s origin.

before.clue: What was Moses told to remove because he was standing on holy ground?
before.fact: Moses was instructed to remove his sandals from his feet before coming any nearer.
before.hint: They covered his feet during a journey.

after.clue: What was Moses told to remove because he was standing on holy ground?
after.fact: Moses was told to remove his sandals because the place was holy ground. The instruction came before his assignment to go to Pharaoh. He first had to respond respectfully to the one speaking to him. (Exodus 3:4–10)
after.hint: They covered his feet during a journey.
after.narration: God calls to Moses and tells him not to come any nearer. Moses must respond to an instruction showing respect for this holy place.

records.reviewNote: Egypt is both the place of suffering and Moses’ assignment. The explanation connects rescue with Jehovah having heard the outcry.

before.clue: To which country was Moses sent to bring his people out?
before.fact: Jehovah said he had heard his people’s outcry and would send Moses to Pharaoh to lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
before.hint: The country Moses had left years earlier.

after.clue: To which country was Moses sent to bring his people out?
after.fact: Jehovah said he had seen the suffering in Egypt and heard the people's outcry. He would send Moses to Pharaoh to bring them out. The assignment began with Jehovah's attention to people in pain. (Exodus 3:7–10)
after.hint: The country Moses had left years earlier.
after.narration: Jehovah says he has seen his people's suffering and heard their outcry. He now gives Moses an assignment to bring them out.

records.reviewNote: Jehovah’s name is tied to the God of the forefathers. The explanation avoids claiming that no one previously knew the name.

before.clue: What personal name did God tell Moses to use when speaking to Israel?
before.fact: Jehovah told Moses that his name was to be remembered from generation to generation.
before.hint: The divine name used throughout the New World Translation.

after.clue: What personal name did God tell Moses to use when speaking to Israel?
after.fact: Jehovah linked his name with the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and said it was to be remembered from generation to generation. Moses' message connected the rescue with the promises made to Israel's forefathers. (Exodus 3:13–17)
after.hint: The divine name used throughout the New World Translation.
after.narration: Moses asks what he should say if the Israelites ask who sent him. God's answer connects his name with the God of their forefathers.

records.reviewNote: The rod becomes a serpent and returns to a rod. The explanation places this sign within Moses’ concern about being believed.

before.clue: What did Moses throw down that became a serpent?
before.fact: Moses threw down his rod and it became a serpent; when he took hold of it as instructed, it became a rod again.
before.hint: A short word for a shepherd’s staff.

after.clue: What did Moses throw down that became a serpent?
after.fact: Moses' rod became a serpent and then became a rod again when he took it by the tail. Jehovah explained the purpose of the sign: to help the people believe that he had appeared to Moses. (Exodus 4:1–5)
after.hint: A short word for a shepherd’s staff.
after.narration: Moses asks what will happen if the people don't believe him. Jehovah gives him a sign using something already in his hand.

records.reviewNote: The hand becomes diseased and is restored. The explanation follows both steps without graphic description.

before.clue: Which part of Moses’ body was affected and then restored as a sign?
before.fact: Moses put his hand inside his garment. When he drew it out, it was diseased; after repeating the action, it was restored.
before.hint: It was placed in the upper fold of his garment.

after.clue: Which part of Moses’ body was affected and then restored as a sign?
after.fact: Moses' hand became diseased and was restored when he repeated the instructed action. Jehovah gave this as another sign in case the people didn't heed the first one. He was preparing Moses to address their doubts. (Exodus 4:6–8)
after.hint: It was placed in the upper fold of his garment.
after.narration: Another sign follows, this time involving Moses' own body. What is affected is then restored.

records.reviewNote: Aaron is appointed to speak with Moses. The explanation preserves Jehovah’s help to both rather than implying Moses is replaced.

before.clue: Which brother was appointed to speak for Moses?
before.fact: Moses worried about speaking. Jehovah said that Moses’ brother Aaron could speak for him.
before.hint: His brother later met him in the wilderness.

after.clue: Which brother was appointed to speak for Moses?
after.fact: Moses said speaking was difficult for him. Jehovah appointed Aaron to speak for him, while Moses would pass on God's words. They had different roles in the same assignment. (Exodus 4:10–16)
after.hint: His brother later met him in the wilderness.
after.narration: Moses explains that speaking is difficult for him. Jehovah names someone who will help him carry the message.

records.reviewNote: The elders hear the words and see the signs; the people believe and bow down. The explanation completes this episode’s return-and-response arc.

before.clue: Whom did Moses and Aaron gather when they returned to the Israelites?
before.fact: Moses and Aaron gathered the elders of Israel. The people believed when they heard that Jehovah had paid attention to their suffering.
before.hint: Older men representing the people of Israel.

after.clue: Whom did Moses and Aaron gather when they returned to the Israelites?
after.fact: Aaron told the elders what Jehovah had said, and the signs were performed before the people. They believed and bowed down when they heard that Jehovah had seen their suffering. The brothers' return brought the message of rescue to the community. (Exodus 4:27–31)
after.hint: Older men representing the people of Israel.
after.narration: The brothers return and gather representatives of the people. The message and signs lead the people to believe and bow down in worship.

records.reviewNote: Priority means going first. Abram’s proposal gives Lot a choice and a practical end to quarreling; inference is labeled in the bank.

before.narration: Abram takes the initiative to preserve peace, inviting Lot to select a direction and agreeing to go the other way.
before.explanation: Abram let Lot choose first rather than demanding the best land for himself (Genesis 13:8–9).

word.clue: What did Abram give up when he allowed Lot to select his land first?
word.explanation: Abram took the initiative to prevent a quarrel and let Lot choose first; the principle is consideration, not weakness.
word.hint1: Abram could have insisted on choosing before his younger relative.
word.hint2: His proposal removed a potential contest over who decided first.

after.narration: Abram asks for the quarreling to stop. He offers Lot the first choice of where to go, and says he'll take the other direction.
after.explanation: Priority means going first. Abram let Lot choose a direction and offered to take the other one. His proposal gave the households a practical way to separate without continuing the quarrel.

word.clue: What did Abram give up when he allowed Lot to select his land first?
word.explanation: Priority means going first. Abram let Lot choose a direction and offered to take the other one. His proposal gave the households a practical way to separate without continuing the quarrel.
word.hint1: Abram could have insisted on choosing before his younger relative.
word.hint2: His proposal removed a potential contest over who decided first.

records.reviewNote: Lot chooses attractive land near wicked men. The explanation observes that contrast without imposing a rule about where every Christian must live.

before.narration: Lot notices the well-watered district of the Jordan and chooses it; he later sets up his tent near Sodom.
before.explanation: Genesis 13:10–13 explains both why the district looked attractive and that the people of Sodom were wicked; it does not explain Lot’s private motive beyond his choice.

word.clue: What important factor besides fertile land should Lot’s decision make us consider?
word.explanation: Lot chose the well-watered district; Genesis immediately reports the wicked conduct of Sodom’s men. Evaluating a place involves more than its appearance.
word.hint1: Genesis describes the land as appealing and its nearby residents very differently.
word.hint2: A beautiful location does not guarantee good human surroundings.

after.narration: Lot notices the well-watered district of the Jordan and chooses it; he later sets up his tent near Sodom.
after.explanation: Lot saw a well-watered region and chose it. Genesis then tells us that Sodom's men were wicked. The contrast gives us two things to notice about a place: its surroundings and the conduct of the people there.

word.clue: The land looked inviting, but Sodom's people were wicked. What do we call the people living near us?
word.explanation: Lot saw a well-watered region and chose it. Genesis then tells us that Sodom's men were wicked. The contrast gives us two things to notice about a place: its surroundings and the conduct of the people there.
word.hint1: Genesis describes the land as appealing and its nearby residents very differently.
word.hint2: A beautiful location does not guarantee good human surroundings.

records.reviewNote: The inheritance promise concerns offspring and long-term possession, not an immediate land transfer. The explanation expands the time horizon.

before.narration: After Lot departs, Jehovah invites Abram to look in every direction and renews the land and offspring promise. Abram later dwells by the big trees of Mamre and builds an altar.
before.explanation: Jehovah repeated the land promise, compared Abram’s offspring to the dust of the earth, and Abram built an altar near Mamre (Genesis 13:14–18).

word.clue: What would Abram’s descendants eventually do with the land Jehovah pointed out?
word.explanation: After Lot separated, Jehovah renewed the promise to give the land to Abram and his offspring. Abram also built an altar in the Hebron/Mamre area.
word.hint1: The promise was about long-term possession, not a single season of grazing.
word.hint2: God spoke about both the territory and Abram’s future offspring.

after.narration: Lot has gone his way. Now Jehovah tells Abram to look north, south, east, and west. The promise concerns all that land—and offspring as numerous as the dust of the earth.
after.explanation: After Lot left, Jehovah invited Abram to look in every direction. He promised the land to Abram and his offspring, and compared their number to the dust of the earth. The promise reached far beyond Abram's present household.

word.clue: What would Abram’s descendants eventually do with the land Jehovah pointed out?
word.explanation: After Lot left, Jehovah invited Abram to look in every direction. He promised the land to Abram and his offspring, and compared their number to the dust of the earth. The promise reached far beyond Abram's present household.
word.hint1: The promise was about long-term possession, not a single season of grazing.
word.hint2: God spoke about both the territory and Abram’s future offspring.

records.reviewNote: Lot is carried off with possessions after the kings’ battle. The hint clarifies captivity without printing the answer.

before.narration: After a battle among kings, the victors carry off goods and provisions; Lot, living in Sodom, is also taken captive with his possessions.
before.explanation: Genesis 14:11–12 specifically records Lot and his possessions being taken when Sodom was plundered.

word.clue: What happened to Lot when the attacking kings carried off Sodom’s goods?
word.explanation: The attacking kings took Lot and his possessions. Genesis does not identify Lot as a soldier in the battle.
word.hint1: The raid affected residents as well as property.
word.hint2: Lot was living in Sodom when its victors departed.

after.narration: A battle among kings reaches Lot's household. The victors take Sodom's goods and food, and carry Lot away with his possessions. How will Abram respond?
after.explanation: Lot was living in Sodom when its goods and provisions were taken. He was carried off with his possessions too. The conflict among the kings had now directly reached Abram's own family.

word.clue: What happened to Lot when the attacking kings carried off Sodom’s goods?
word.explanation: Lot was living in Sodom when its goods and provisions were taken. He was carried off with his possessions too. The conflict among the kings had now directly reached Abram's own family.
word.hint1: The raid affected residents as well as property.
word.hint2: He wasn't free to return home; the victors carried him away with their takings.

records.reviewNote: The 318 household men are trained. Night action and divided forces make the rescue explanation teach planning as well as pursuit.

before.narration: A survivor tells Abram what happened. Abram gathers 318 trained men from his household, pursues the raiders, and brings Lot and the others back.
before.explanation: Genesis 14:14 records 318 trained men born in Abram’s household; the passage reports that Abram recovered Lot and others.

word.clue: What kind of household men did Abram mobilize for Lot’s rescue?
word.explanation: Abram took 318 trained men born in his household, pursued the captors, and recovered Lot and the possessions.
word.hint1: The rescuers were connected to his own household, not described as a hired foreign army.
word.hint2: Genesis counts 318 such men before the pursuit.

after.narration: A survivor tells Abram what happened. Abram gathers 318 trained men from his household, pursues the raiders, and brings Lot and the others back.
after.explanation: Abram took 318 trained men born in his household. He divided his forces and attacked at night, then brought back Lot, the goods, and the other people. The rescue involved planning as well as pursuit.

word.clue: What kind of household men did Abram take to rescue Lot?
word.explanation: Abram took 318 trained men born in his household. He divided his forces and attacked at night, then brought back Lot, the goods, and the other people. The rescue involved planning as well as pursuit.
word.hint1: The rescuers were connected to his own household, not described as a hired foreign army.
word.hint2: These men had already been prepared for action; they weren't starting from scratch.

records.reviewNote: Melchizedek is king and priest. The new hint uses Abram’s tenth and the explanation connects the blessing with worship.

before.narration: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, brings bread and wine and blesses Abram after his victory.
before.explanation: Melchizedek is described as both king of Salem and priest of the Most High God; Abram gives him a tenth of everything (Genesis 14:18–20).

word.clue: Besides being king of Salem, what office did Melchizedek hold?
word.explanation: Melchizedek was both king and priest of the Most High God. Hebrews 7 later uses his role to illuminate Jesus’ priesthood.
word.hint1: His unusual dual role later becomes important in Hebrews chapter 7.
word.hint2: His blessing acknowledged the Most High God.

after.narration: After the rescue, Abram meets Melchizedek, the king of Salem. He brings bread and wine and blesses Abram. But being a king isn't his only role.
after.explanation: Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of the Most High God. He blessed Abram and credited God with handing over the enemies, and Abram gave him a tenth. Their meeting brought worship into the account of the rescue.

word.clue: Besides being king of Salem, what office did Melchizedek hold?
word.explanation: Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of the Most High God. He blessed Abram and credited God with handing over the enemies, and Abram gave him a tenth. Their meeting brought worship into the account of the rescue.
word.hint1: Abram gave him a tenth of the recovered goods after their meeting.
word.hint2: He held an office in the worship of the Most High God and pronounced a blessing on Abram.

records.reviewNote: Spoils means goods taken in war. Abram refuses his own enrichment while protecting his companions’ portions; no blanket ban on all recovered property.

before.narration: The king of Sodom offers goods to Abram, but Abram refuses to take anything for himself, while preserving the rightful shares of his allies.
before.explanation: Abram declined the king’s offered enrichment but explicitly allowed his companions their portions (Genesis 14:22–24).

word.clue: What did Abram refuse to keep so Sodom’s king could not claim to enrich him?
word.explanation: Abram would not keep the king of Sodom’s goods as personal gain, so the king could not claim credit for making him wealthy.
word.hint1: The decision came after the rescue, when recovered valuables were offered.
word.hint2: Abram did distinguish his own share from the portions owed to his companions.

after.narration: The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods. Abram won't keep them for himself, but asks that his companions receive their portions.
after.explanation: Spoils are goods taken in war. Abram refused the king's offer so the king couldn't claim to have made him rich. But he protected the portions due to his companions. His decision about his own share didn't cancel theirs.

word.clue: What did Abram refuse to keep so Sodom’s king could not claim to enrich him?
word.explanation: Spoils are goods taken in war. Abram refused the king's offer so the king couldn't claim to have made him rich. But he protected the portions due to his companions. His decision about his own share didn't cancel theirs.
word.hint1: The decision came after the rescue, when recovered valuables were offered.
word.hint2: Abram did distinguish his own share from the portions owed to his companions.

records.reviewNote: Ishmael means God Hears. The revised clue asks for the son rather than an ambiguous well association; the message precedes his birth.

before.narration: Sarai gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife. Tensions and humiliation follow, and pregnant Hagar flees. Jehovah’s angel finds her by a wilderness spring, speaks of her son Ishmael, and Hagar later bears him to Abram.
before.explanation: Genesis 16:7–11 says the angel found Hagar by a spring and told her to name her future son Ishmael; Genesis 16:15–16 records his later birth when Abram was 86.

word.clue: What name was chosen because Jehovah had heard Hagar’s affliction?
word.explanation: The angel instructed Hagar to name her son Ishmael, meaning “God Hears.” The nearby well was called Beer-lahai-roi, a different name.
word.hint1: The explanation comes from the angel before the boy was born.
word.hint2: Its meaning is connected with being listened to, not with the nearby well’s name.

after.narration: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife. When Hagar becomes pregnant, the household conflict grows, and she flees. Jehovah's angel finds her by a wilderness spring with a message about her son.
after.explanation: Ishmael means God Hears. The angel told Hagar to use that name because Jehovah had heard her affliction. The message reached her at a wilderness spring, before her son had even been born.

word.clue: What name did the angel tell Hagar to give her son because Jehovah had heard her affliction?
word.explanation: Ishmael means God Hears. The angel told Hagar to use that name because Jehovah had heard her affliction. The message reached her at a wilderness spring, before her son had even been born.
word.hint1: The explanation comes from the angel before the boy was born.
word.hint2: Its meaning is connected with being listened to, not with the nearby well’s name.

records.reviewNote: Abraham’s name points to a crowd or multitude. NWT footnotes also support Sarah’s meaning; the clue now defines the requested vocabulary.

before.narration: God changes Abram’s name to Abraham and Sarai’s to Sarah. He confirms that Sarah will have a son named Isaac and gives Abraham further covenant instructions.
before.explanation: Jehovah gave prophetic significance to these names: Abraham ('Father of a Multitude') would father nations; Sarah ('Princess') would become an ancestress of kings; and Isaac means 'Laughter' (Genesis 17:5–6, 15–19; NWT footnotes).

word.clue: What does the key idea in Abram’s new name, Abraham, refer to?
word.explanation: Abraham’s name means “Father of a Crowd (Multitude); Father of Many.” Sarah’s new name means “Princess.”
word.hint1: The change pointed forward to something far larger than one son.
word.hint2: Jehovah said he would make Abraham a father of many nations.

after.narration: Abram and Sarai receive new names: Abraham and Sarah. Jehovah promises a son through Sarah, tells them to name him Isaac, and gives Abraham instructions about the covenant.
after.explanation: Abraham means Father of a Crowd, or Multitude. Jehovah connected the new name with a promise of many nations and kings. Sarah's name means Princess, and the promise specifically included a son through her.

word.clue: Abraham's new name pictured him as the father of a ___. What word means a large crowd?
word.explanation: Abraham means Father of a Crowd, or Multitude. Jehovah connected the new name with a promise of many nations and kings. Sarah's name means Princess, and the promise specifically included a son through her.
word.hint1: The change pointed forward to something far larger than one son.
word.hint2: Jehovah said he would make Abraham a father of many nations.

records.reviewNote: Welcome is a semantic summary, not a quotation. Water, food, rest and the help of Sarah and an attendant ground the application in actual actions.

before.narration: Abraham welcomes three visitors under the trees of Mamre, arranging water for their feet, shade and rest, bread, and food.
before.explanation: Abraham hurried to provide water, food and hospitality for the three men (Genesis 18:1–8).

word.clue: What did Abraham extend to the three visitors through his generous hospitality?
word.explanation: Abraham hurried to receive the visitors and arranged food, water, and rest. His actions illustrate practical hospitality.
word.hint1: Abraham invited the visitors to stay, rest, wash, and eat instead of walking past.
word.hint2: His warmth was more than a meal—he made strangers feel received and cared for.

after.narration: Three visitors arrive near Abraham's tent. He hurries to arrange water for their feet, a place to rest, and a meal. Let's look at how he receives them.
after.explanation: Abraham hurried to provide water, food, and rest for the visitors. He involved Sarah and an attendant in preparing the meal. His welcome was something he put into action, not just a greeting.

word.clue: What simple word sums up Abraham's generous reception of the visitors?
word.explanation: Abraham hurried to provide water, food, and rest for the visitors. He involved Sarah and an attendant in preparing the meal. His welcome was something he put into action, not just a greeting.
word.hint1: He hurried to arrange water and a meal when they arrived.
word.hint2: Think of the greeting that tells a visitor they're invited to stay.

records.reviewNote: Lot’s lingering triggers angelic assistance explicitly attributed to Jehovah’s compassion. The explanation adds the reason for the rescue.

before.narration: The angels urge Lot and his family to flee. Lot, his wife, and two daughters are led away; Lot reaches Zoar, while his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
before.explanation: Genesis 19:15–26 describes Lot, his wife, and two daughters leaving and his wife looking back; 19:29 notes Abraham was remembered in the deliverance.

word.clue: What did Lot do despite the urgent warning, prompting angels to take the family by the hand?
word.explanation: Lot lingered; the angels took him and his family by the hand and brought them outside. He later asked to go to Zoar.
word.hint1: The danger had been stated, but departure was delayed.
word.hint2: Genesis 19 describes divine mercy during that delay.

after.narration: The warning is urgent: Lot and his family must leave. The angels lead them away, and Lot reaches Zoar. His wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
after.explanation: Lot lingered, and the angels took him and his family by the hand to lead them out. Genesis says they did this because of Jehovah's compassion for him. Their rescue shows mercy in action.

word.clue: What did Lot do despite the urgent warning, prompting angels to take the family by the hand?
word.explanation: Lot lingered, and the angels took him and his family by the hand to lead them out. Genesis says they did this because of Jehovah's compassion for him. Their rescue shows mercy in action.
word.hint1: The danger had been stated, but departure was delayed.
word.hint2: Genesis 19 describes divine mercy during that delay.

records.reviewNote: Isaac is born at the appointed time with Abraham aged 100. The explanation connects Sarah’s laughter to the fulfilled promise.

before.narration: At the appointed time Sarah gives birth to Isaac. Abraham is 100 years old, and Sarah joyfully speaks of laughter.
before.explanation: Genesis 21:1–7 says Sarah bore Isaac when Abraham was 100, and Sarah spoke joyfully of laughter.

word.clue: Jehovah’s promise that Sarah would have a son was _________ at the appointed time.
word.explanation: Isaac’s birth fulfilled Jehovah’s promise at the appointed time; Abraham was 100 years old.
word.hint1: Jehovah had told Abraham and Sarah when their son would arrive.
word.hint2: When Isaac was born, the promise was no longer just a prediction.

after.narration: At the appointed time Sarah gives birth to Isaac. Abraham is 100 years old, and Sarah joyfully speaks of laughter.
after.explanation: Isaac was born at the appointed time, just as Jehovah had promised. Abraham was 100 years old, and Sarah spoke about the laughter his birth brought. A promise they'd waited for had become part of their family life.

word.clue: Jehovah’s promise that Sarah would have a son was _________ at the appointed time.
word.explanation: Isaac was born at the appointed time, just as Jehovah had promised. Abraham was 100 years old, and Sarah spoke about the laughter his birth brought. A promise they'd waited for had become part of their family life.
word.hint1: Jehovah had told Abraham and Sarah when their son would arrive.
word.hint2: When Isaac was born, the promise was no longer just a prediction.

records.reviewNote: Hagar receives reassurance before seeing water. The new explanation preserves the order and God’s hearing of the boy.

before.narration: After Isaac is weaned, Sarah sees Ishmael mocking Isaac. Abraham is distressed but follows God’s instruction. Hagar and her son are sent away; in the wilderness their water runs out, God hears the boy, and Hagar notices a well and gives him water.
before.explanation: Genesis 21:14–19 describes Hagar with her son, an exhausted water supply, God hearing Ishmael, and the revealed well. He is older than a baby at this point; his birth occurred before Isaac’s.

word.clue: What did the angel do for Hagar before Jehovah opened her eyes to water?
word.explanation: God heard the boy; the angel reassured Hagar about his future, and God enabled her to see a well. The passage does not say water miraculously appeared.
word.hint1: Her distress and her son’s future were both addressed.
word.hint2: The message said God had heard the boy and described his future.

after.narration: After Isaac is weaned, Sarah sees Ishmael mocking Isaac. Abraham is distressed but follows God’s instruction. Hagar and her son are sent away; in the wilderness their water runs out, God hears the boy, and Hagar notices a well and gives him water.
after.explanation: Before Hagar saw the well, the angel told her not to be afraid and promised that her son would become a great nation. God had heard the boy. Hagar then filled the water bag and gave him a drink.

word.clue: What did the angel do for Hagar before Jehovah opened her eyes to water?
word.explanation: Before Hagar saw the well, the angel told her not to be afraid and promised that her son would become a great nation. God had heard the boy. Hagar then filled the water bag and gave him a drink.
word.hint1: Her distress and her son’s future were both addressed.
word.hint2: The message said God had heard the boy and described his future.

records.reviewNote: Genesis 22:1 identifies a test. The explanation follows preparation and the servants’ departure without inventing Isaac’s age or emotions.

before.narration: Abraham obeys a difficult instruction concerning Isaac and journeys toward the region of Moriah, carrying what is required. He leaves two attendants with the donkey as he and Isaac continue.
before.explanation: Genesis 22:3–5 records Abraham splitting wood and traveling with Isaac and two attendants; the attendants remain with the donkey.

word.clue: Jehovah gave Abraham a difficult instruction about Isaac as a way of _______ his faith.
word.explanation: Genesis 22:1 identifies the event as a test. Jehovah’s angel stopped Abraham before Isaac was harmed.
word.hint1: Genesis 22:1 identifies the purpose before describing what Abraham was asked to do.
word.hint2: The command revealed how deeply Abraham trusted and obeyed Jehovah.

after.narration: Abraham receives a difficult instruction about Isaac. He prepares for the journey toward Moriah and sets out with his son and two servants. Later, he and Isaac go on while the servants stay with the donkey.
after.explanation: Genesis tells us from the start that this was a test. Abraham prepared the wood and set out with Isaac and two servants. Later, he and Isaac continued without the servants. The account lets us follow his obedience step by step.

word.clue: Jehovah gave Abraham a difficult instruction about Isaac as a way of _______ his faith.
word.explanation: Genesis tells us from the start that this was a test. Abraham prepared the wood and set out with Isaac and two servants. Later, he and Isaac continued without the servants. The account lets us follow his obedience step by step.
word.hint1: Genesis 22:1 identifies the purpose before describing what Abraham was asked to do.
word.hint2: The command revealed how deeply Abraham trusted and obeyed Jehovah.

records.reviewNote: The ram is caught by its horns in a thicket. The hints describe vegetation and the explanation accurately explains Jehovah-jireh.

before.narration: Abraham prepares to obey, but an angel calls out and stops him. He then sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead of Isaac.
before.explanation: Genesis 22:11–13 says the angel stopped Abraham and a ram caught by its horns was offered instead.

word.clue: Where was the substitute ram caught when Abraham looked up?
word.explanation: The ram was caught by its horns in a thicket, and Abraham offered it in place of Isaac.
word.hint1: The substitute was not brought by another person.
word.hint2: Genesis identifies what held the ram by its horns.

after.narration: Abraham prepares to obey, but an angel calls out and stops him. He then sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead of Isaac.
after.explanation: The angel stopped Abraham before Isaac was harmed. Abraham then saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket and offered it instead of his son. He named the place Jehovah-jireh, meaning Jehovah Will Provide.

word.clue: Where was the substitute ram caught when Abraham looked up?
word.explanation: The angel stopped Abraham before Isaac was harmed. Abraham then saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket and offered it instead of his son. He named the place Jehovah-jireh, meaning Jehovah Will Provide.
word.hint1: It was a dense patch of vegetation, rather than a building or an animal enclosure.
word.hint2: The ram's horns were caught among the growth, so it couldn't get free.

records.reviewNote: All nations can obtain a blessing through the offspring. The explanation keeps this broader future promise distinct from one household’s rescue.

before.narration: Jehovah repeats the promise to Abraham that his offspring will become numerous and that all nations can receive a blessing through his offspring.
before.explanation: Genesis 22:15–18 reaffirms numerous offspring and blessing for all nations; distinguish the promise from later fulfillment.

word.clue: Who beyond Abraham’s own family would be blessed by means of his offspring?
word.explanation: Jehovah said all nations of the earth could obtain a blessing by means of Abraham’s offspring.
word.hint1: The promise is global rather than limited to one household.
word.hint2: The wording of Genesis 22:18 reaches people throughout the earth.

after.narration: After Abraham obeys, Jehovah repeats the promise about his offspring. The blessing won't stop with one family. Notice how far it will reach.
after.explanation: Jehovah repeated the promise after Abraham had obeyed: people of all nations could obtain a blessing through his offspring. The promise reached beyond one family, and beyond the events Abraham himself would live to see.

word.clue: Who beyond Abraham’s own family would be blessed by means of his offspring?
word.explanation: Jehovah repeated the promise after Abraham had obeyed: people of all nations could obtain a blessing through his offspring. The promise reached beyond one family, and beyond the events Abraham himself would live to see.
word.hint1: The promise is global rather than limited to one household.
word.hint2: The wording of Genesis 22:18 reaches people throughout the earth.

records.reviewNote: The field and cave are purchased for 400 silver shekels before witnesses. Compound references also introduce the later marriage mission.

before.narration: Sarah dies at 127, and Abraham mourns her and arranges for her burial in the cave of Machpelah. Later Abraham asks his senior household servant to seek a wife for Isaac from Abraham’s relatives.
before.explanation: Genesis 23:1–20 records Sarah’s death and burial; Genesis 24:1–4 gives Abraham’s instructions to his servant.

word.clue: What did Abraham insist on completing for Sarah’s burial property, rather than simply accepting it free?
word.explanation: Abraham paid for the field and cave of Machpelah before witnesses. This was a formal purchase, not merely permission to bury Sarah.
word.hint1: The agreement was made publicly with witnesses.
word.hint2: He weighed out silver for the field and cave.

after.narration: Sarah dies at 127. Abraham mourns her and arranges to buy a burial place at Machpelah. Later, he sends his servant to his relatives to find a wife for Isaac.
after.explanation: Abraham paid 400 silver shekels before witnesses, and the field and cave became his property. The purchase gave him a burial place for Sarah as a settled possession. The account carefully records both the payment and the transfer.

word.clue: What did Abraham insist on completing for Sarah's burial property, rather than accepting it as a gift?
word.explanation: Abraham paid 400 silver shekels before witnesses, and the field and cave became his property. The purchase gave him a burial place for Sarah as a settled possession. The account carefully records both the payment and the transfer.
word.hint1: The agreement was made publicly with witnesses.
word.hint2: He weighed out silver for the field and cave.

records.reviewNote: The servant prays and observes Rebekah quietly. Guidance is a fair inference from the request and subsequent watchfulness.

before.narration: Near the city, the servant has his camels kneel beside a well at evening and prays for a young woman who will offer water to him and also his camels.
before.explanation: Genesis 24:11–14 places the servant by a well at evening and records his request for a woman willing to water both him and the camels.

word.clue: What was the servant seeking when he prayed before approaching women at the well?
word.explanation: The servant prayed for success and a sign of loyal love to Abraham. He used an observable offer of hospitality rather than claiming to read private motives.
word.hint1: He did not rely merely on family ties or a stranger’s appearance.
word.hint2: His request named observable conduct that would reveal hospitable initiative.

after.narration: It's evening when the servant reaches the well outside the city. He has the camels kneel down and prays. He asks that the woman chosen for Isaac offer water for him and his camels.
after.explanation: Rebekah arrived before the servant had finished speaking. He then watched quietly to see whether Jehovah had made his journey successful. His prayer was followed by careful attention to what happened.

word.clue: What was the servant seeking when he prayed before approaching women at the well?
word.explanation: Rebekah arrived before the servant had finished speaking. He then watched quietly to see whether Jehovah had made his journey successful. His prayer was followed by careful attention to what happened.
word.hint1: He asked Jehovah for help before speaking to the young woman.
word.hint2: He asked for a response he could observe: an offer to water both him and his camels.

records.reviewNote: Diligence is supported by repeated drawing for the camels without a request. The explanation defines the quality and shows the work behind it.

before.narration: Rebekah gives the servant a drink and volunteers to draw water for all his camels. She repeatedly draws and pours until the camels have enough.
before.explanation: Genesis 24:18–20 emphasizes Rebekah’s initiative and that she ran repeatedly to draw sufficient water for all the camels.

word.clue: What quality did Rebekah demonstrate by repeatedly drawing water until the camels finished?
word.explanation: Rebekah voluntarily watered the camels until they were finished, showing generous effort. Genesis does not specify exactly how many trips she made.
word.hint1: The servant only asked for water for himself.
word.hint2: The extra task required sustained effort without being requested.

after.narration: Rebekah gives the servant a drink, then offers to water all his camels too. She keeps running back to draw more until they've finished drinking. There's real effort behind this act of kindness!
after.explanation: Diligence is steady, careful effort. Rebekah offered water for the camels without being asked and kept running back to the well until they had all drunk. That was generosity backed by hard work!

word.clue: What quality did Rebekah demonstrate by repeatedly drawing water until the camels finished?
word.explanation: Diligence is steady, careful effort. Rebekah offered water for the camels without being asked and kept running back to the well until they had all drunk. That was generosity backed by hard work!
word.hint1: The servant only asked for water for himself.
word.hint2: The extra task required sustained effort without being requested.

records.reviewNote: The retelling in Genesis 24:47 puts identity before putting on jewelry. Revised narration follows that order; the extra verse range is linked correctly.

before.narration: After the camels finish drinking, the servant gives Rebekah a gold nose ring and two bracelets, asks her family connection, and learns there is room to lodge.
before.explanation: Genesis 24:22–27 specifies a gold nose ring and two bracelets and describes Rebekah’s family and hospitality.

word.clue: What did the servant do after learning Rebekah’s family connection and reflecting on Jehovah’s help?
word.explanation: The servant bowed down before Jehovah and praised him for his loyal love and guidance (Genesis 24:26–27).
word.hint1: His first response was directed toward Jehovah, not toward the gifts.
word.hint2: He bowed low before describing his mission to the household.

after.narration: The servant asks about Rebekah's family and whether there's a place to lodge. He gives her gold jewelry and bows to thank Jehovah for guiding him.

sceneIntroductions.narration: Before the six creative periods are described, Genesis introduces the heavens and the earth. It doesn't give a date for their creation.
Light reaches the earth, and day becomes distinguishable from night. Insight explains that light could reach the surface before its sources were clearly visible from there.
Jehovah separates waters below from waters above and gives the space between them a name. Picture how the scene is changing.
The waters collect into seas and dry ground appears. The earth is being prepared for the life that will follow.
Vegetation and fruit trees begin to grow. Jehovah's direction also describes how this plant life will keep reproducing.
The heavenly lights mark a rhythm of time for life on earth. Their role reaches beyond simply making the sky bright.
Now the waters are to teem with living creatures. Genesis includes great sea creatures as well as the life swarming around them.
The creatures of sea and sky receive a blessing. The account looks ahead to the generations of living things that will follow.
The land is filled with different groups of animals. Notice the several kinds of creatures named in the account.
The first humans are made in God's image and receive responsibilities toward the earth and its animals. Their place in this home comes with work to do.
Jehovah prepares a beautiful home with trees that are pleasing to look at and good for food. Adam is also given work caring for it.
Water flows through this home and then divides into four named waterways. Genesis pauses to describe the surrounding lands too.
Adam has abundant food available to him. Jehovah gives one clear restriction, with a warning about what disobedience would bring.
Adam names the animals, but no suitable companion for him has been found. Jehovah says it isn't good for the man to continue alone.
A question now challenges what Jehovah said. Soon an outright contradiction follows, putting trust in his word at the center of the account.
Eve listens to the claim, looks at what has been forbidden, and eats. Adam joins her. Their choices have consequences for the home they've been given.
Adam and Eve leave their home. Access to the tree of life is now blocked, and the account describes the protection placed at its entrance.
Eve has her first son and speaks of Jehovah's help. The story of the next generation begins with this birth and the younger brother who follows.
The brothers grow up doing different work. One cultivates the ground; the other tends living creatures.
What Cain brings to Jehovah comes from the ground he works. Let's follow the connection between his everyday work and his gift.
Both brothers bring something to Jehovah, but they don't receive the same response. The account makes us look beyond the outward act alone.
Hebrews later looks back at Abel's worship and tells us what made his sacrifice of greater worth. It gives us an important detail beyond his occupation.
Cain becomes angry and dejected. Jehovah speaks to him while there is still an opportunity to turn to doing good.
Jehovah describes sin as something crouching at the door. Cain is being urged to get mastery over it before taking another step.
Cain invites Abel to go with him. The warning has already been given, but Cain now makes a choice that ends his brother's life.
Jehovah asks Cain where Abel is. Cain's reply tries to avoid responsibility, but the next words show that what happened is known.
Cain's wrongdoing affects the ground he cultivated and the life he will lead. He can no longer treat the consequences as something left behind in one place.
The earth is full of violence, yet one man is described as walking with the true God. The rescue account begins with the life he is already leading.
Jehovah gives detailed building instructions before the Flood comes. Responding to the warning means preparing a very large vessel.
The human passengers enter together: a husband and wife, their three sons, and the sons' wives. Their rescue is a shared household story.
The preparations include living creatures of many kinds and food to sustain them. Life after the Flood is already part of the rescue arrangements.
The time of preparation ends and the floodwaters come. One part of the account lasts forty days and forty nights.
The waters rise until the mountains are covered. The vessel stays afloat while the world outside it is overwhelmed.
The vessel comes to rest in a mountainous region, but the waiting isn't over. The waters continue to recede before the ground is ready.
After sending out a raven, Noah sends another bird to check conditions. Its journeys provide clues about the land outside.
A bird returns with a freshly plucked leaf. That small detail tells Noah something important about the retreating water.
After leaving the vessel, the survivors receive a promise concerning future generations. Jehovah gives a visible sign in the clouds.
People share one language and begin a large building project together. Their ability to understand one another makes the plan possible.
The builders settle on a broad plain. This land will remain linked with Babel in later Bible history.
The people make their own building material and bake it with fire. Their project uses something different from ordinary stone.
The baked blocks need to be joined together. The account names the material that serves as their mortar.
The plan includes a whole settlement as well as a tall structure. The builders say they don't want to be scattered across the earth.
The builders want a structure with its top in the heavens. Their own words connect the project with a wish for fame.
Listen to the ambition the builders state for themselves. Their aim concerns how they will be known, as well as where they will live.
Jehovah acts on the ability that has made their cooperation possible. People who had understood one another can no longer do so.
Construction stops and the people spread out. The very outcome they'd wanted to prevent becomes part of the story.
The city receives a name connected with what happened to the people's language. Genesis ties the name to Jehovah's action.
Terah's household leaves Ur with Canaan as its destination. Abram travels with Sarai and his nephew Lot.
The family settles along the way instead of reaching Canaan in one move. After Terah's death, Abram will continue the journey.
Sarai has no child, yet Jehovah makes a promise about a people who will come from Abram. The promise looks far beyond the household as it is now.
Jehovah's words reach beyond Abram's own descendants. People throughout the earth are included in the blessing he describes.
Abram leaves with his wife and nephew, along with their possessions and the people they'd acquired. This is a household on the move.
A younger relative travels with Abram. Their shared journey will lead to important decisions about where their households live.
The travelers reach the land Jehovah promised to show Abram. Other people already live there, and the promise still looks ahead to his offspring.
Abram stops near the big trees of Moreh. Here Jehovah appears to him and speaks about giving the land to his offspring.
After Jehovah appears to Abram, Abram builds something used in worship. It marks this stage of his journey before he moves on.
Abram pitches his tent between two towns, with Ai to the east. He again builds an altar and calls on Jehovah's name.
A mother has kept her baby concealed for three months. When she can no longer do so, she prepares a coated papyrus container and places him among the riverbank plants.
The prepared container is placed along the bank of Egypt's great river. Pharaoh's daughter will come down to bathe in the same place.
The baby has been placed at the river's edge, among the plants growing there. His sister watches from a distance.
A member of the baby's own family stays nearby to see what will happen. Her attention will soon lead to a chance to help.
The watching sister steps forward when Pharaoh's daughter finds the baby. Another Bible passage identifies this sister by name.
A woman from Pharaoh's household sees the crying Hebrew baby and feels compassion. She is willing to hear the sister's suggestion about finding a nurse.
Pharaoh's daughter sends an attendant to get the container. The baby's sister has a different part to play in what follows.
Moses goes out to see the burdens his own people are bearing. He encounters an act of harsh treatment.
Moses intervenes and kills the man who has been beating one of his people. He hides the body, but the incident will become known.
The report reaches Egypt's ruler, and Moses' life is threatened. Staying in Egypt is no longer safe for him.
Moses escapes from Egypt and stops by a well in another land. This stop introduces the people who will become part of his new life.
Seven daughters of a local priest arrive to draw water for their father's flock. Moses is sitting at the place where they come to work.
The women are driven away from the water. Moses gets up to help them and waters their flock.
The daughters get home earlier than usual. Their father asks why, hears about Moses' help, and tells them to invite him for a meal.
Moses agrees to stay with the household. The priest gives one of his daughters to him in marriage.
Moses becomes a father and names his son with his life in another land in view. The account explains the name through Moses' own words.
Back in Egypt, the Israelites continue to groan under slavery. The account turns to God's attention to their suffering and his covenant.
Moses is working as a shepherd for his father-in-law Jethro. As he leads the animals through the wilderness, he reaches Horeb.
Moses reaches the mountain called the mountain of the true God. Here something unusual catches his attention.
Moses sees flames, yet the plant in their midst isn't being consumed. He goes closer to investigate.
God calls to Moses and tells him not to come any nearer. Moses must respond to an instruction showing respect for this holy place.
Jehovah says he has seen his people's suffering and heard their outcry. He now gives Moses an assignment to bring them out.
Moses asks what he should say if the Israelites ask who sent him. God's answer connects his name with the God of their forefathers.
Moses asks what will happen if the people don't believe him. Jehovah gives him a sign using something already in his hand.
Another sign follows, this time involving Moses' own body. What is affected is then restored.
Moses explains that speaking is difficult for him. Jehovah names someone who will help him carry the message.
The brothers return and gather representatives of the people. The message and signs lead the people to believe and bow down in worship.

finales.genesis_ep09: Water shared at a well leads to a new family—and comfort for Isaac.
